ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure is a waveform graph of a sinusoidal alternating current i varying with time t, with the vertical axis labeled i/mA and the horizontal axis labeled t/ms. The positive peak value of the waveform is labeled as 2 mA; at t=0, the curve is near i=√2 mA and is rising. The figure also marks with a dashed line that at t=5 ms, the current is likewise √2 mA, but at this time the curve is on the descending segment. Reasoning: Let the current expression be i(t)=I_m sin(ωt+φ). From the positive peak value in the graph, I_m=2 mA can be obtained. At t=0, i(0)=√2 mA, so 2 sin φ=√2, that is, sin φ=√2/2. Also because the curve is rising at t=0, cos φ>0, therefore φ=45°. At t=5 ms, the current is still √2 mA, but the curve is descending, corresponding to a sine phase of 135°. From t=0 to t=5 ms, the phase increases from 45° to 135°, and the phase difference is 90°=π/2 rad. Therefore ω=(π/2)/(5×10^-3)=100π≈314 rad/s. Thus the analytical expression of the current is i(t)=2 sin(314t+45°) mA.

raw_record.question_text: What is the analytical expression of the AC current \(i(t)\) in the circuit shown in the figure?

method.method_draft: First describe the image as a sinusoidal current-time graph. Take the peak value 2 mA as I_m. Model the waveform as i(t)=I_m sin(omega t+phi). Use the initial point: at t=0, i=sqrt(2) mA and the curve is rising, so phi=45 degrees. Use the dashed point at t=5 ms: the same current value sqrt(2) mA occurs while descending, so the phase there is 135 degrees. The phase change over 5 ms is 90 degrees, giving omega=314 rad/s. Hence write i(t)=2 sin(314t+45 degrees) mA.
